id: Love Poem So Tall It Ends in Heaven

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A man I loved kept a folded square of masking tape in his pocket He did this / only for a year His masking tape was bright orange and fraying As evidence / coroners had used it to attach to his father’s calf the rope his father’d used / This man planted the tape in our yard when the year was done and from it grew thirteen beams / From these beams rafters grew Ropes uncurled from these rafters and fathers hanged from the ropes / Over the fathers a roof blossomed like a shield and against it a ladder leaned / The ladder was so tall the man I loved said it must have ended in heaven And down / from the ladder an angel scurried while we slept In its mouth it carried torn strips / of tape The angel pressed this tape on the calves of the man I loved like bandages / Each morning I removed the tape I was careful not to wake him Each morning / he’d walk through the garden of swaying fathers He’d kneel beside our rosemary bush / He’d rub its leaves in his hands He’d ball his hands in his hair to scent it He wanted / just to keep his earthliness with him / In hell this is the only prerequisite

outputs.L2:
Here's a rewritten version maintaining the original facts and imagery while using different language and phrasing:

For exactly twelve months, the man I loved carried a small, folded piece of masking tape in his pocket—orange, worn thin at the edges. This scrap had once served as evidence: coroners had used it to bind the rope to his father's leg, the same rope his father had chosen to end his life with.

When that year finally ended, he buried the tape in our garden. From that patch of earth, thirteen wooden posts rose up, and from those posts came crossbeams. Coiled ropes unfurled themselves from the rafters, and fathers—plural, unnamed—hung suspended from each one. Above them all, a roof unfolded like protection, like something meant to guard rather than trap them. Leaning against this roof stood a ladder so impossibly tall that the man I loved insisted it must reach all the way to paradise.

At night, while we slept, an angel would descend that ladder, clutching torn pieces of tape between its teeth. It would press these fragments against his calves, like makeshift bandages meant to heal something unspeakable.

Every morning, before he woke, I'd peel away the tape as gently as I could. Then he'd wander through that strange garden where the fathers swayed gently in the breeze. He'd stop at our rosemary bush, crouch beside it, crush its leaves between his palms, then work his scented fingers through his hair—desperate to hold onto some proof of being alive, of belonging to this world.

Because in hell, that's the only thing required of you.
outputs.L3:
**The Garden of Orange Tape**

For a year, the man carried a single folded strip of orange masking tape in his pocket, its edges softened from constant handling, its color dulled by the oil of his fingers. It was the same tape the coroners had used months before—wound around his father's calf to secure the rope that had ended his life, marked and cataloged as evidence before it was finally released back into the world, stripped of its official purpose but heavy with everything it had witnessed. He kept it close the way some men keep photographs or letters, an object made unbearably significant by proximity to death.

When the year had passed, he did not discard it, nor did he frame it or bury it in some private ceremony of closure. Instead, he planted it in the yard, pressing it into the soil as though it were a seed rather than a scrap of adhesive plastic. And impossibly, it took root. From that small orange strip grew beams and rafters, splintered wood rising toward the sky, and from these beams hung ropes—coil after coil, each one bearing the invisible weight of a father who had chosen to leave. The yard became a garden unlike any other, a place where grief did not wilt or fade with the seasons but grew instead into architecture, into structure, into something the man could walk through and touch.

Over this strange garden of loss, a roof formed on its own, sheltering the beams and ropes from wind and rain as though the earth itself understood the fragility of what grew there. Against one side leaned a ladder so impossibly tall that its top disappeared into cloud and light, seeming to pierce the boundary between earth and heaven itself. Each night, an angel descended this ladder—not to speak, not to offer grand pronouncements of comfort, but simply to kneel beside the sleeping man and press small torn pieces of orange tape onto his calves, one after another, like bandages laid over wounds that had never fully closed.

Each morning, before the man woke, the speaker—who watched over this ritual, who perhaps loved him in some quiet, unspoken way—would carefully peel the tape from his skin, careful not to disturb his sleep, careful not to let him see the evidence of what visited him in the dark. Then the man would rise and walk barefoot through his garden of beams and ropes, moving past the architecture of his father's death until he reached a rosemary bush growing at its edge. There he would kneel, breaking off a sprig, crushing it between his palms, and rubbing its sharp, clean scent into his hair, as if trying to carry something living and fragrant into a day that would otherwise smell only of old wood and orange adhesive.

This daily ritual—the planting, the nightly visitation, the careful removal of tape, the rosemary pressed into his hair—was never simply about mourning. It was about tending. The man had built, without entirely meaning to, a shrine to his own survival, a system of small acts that let him hold his grief without being consumed by it. To let the tape grow into a garden rather than remain a single suffocating object; to allow an angel to bandage wounds that medicine could not touch; to walk each morning toward something green and living and fragrant—this was how he kept himself tethered to the earth. It suggested a quiet truth: that survival after such loss requires not forgetting, not erasing the wound, but finding some way to let it grow alongside you, tended daily, until grief and life become inseparable parts of the same garden.
outputs.L4:
# The Orange Tape

The coroner gave it to him in a small plastic bag, as if it were something precious: a strip of orange masking tape, three inches long, fraying at both ends where it had been cut from the rope. This is standard evidence, they said. For the file. He signed something. He does not remember what he signed.

He carried it in his shirt pocket for a year. Not hidden, exactly—just present, the way a held breath is present. He carried it to work, to his mother's house, to the funeral he could not remember attending though photographs proved he had stood there in a black coat, his face doing the thing faces do when they perform grief for other people's comfort. The tape grew softer with handling, the orange dulling to the color of old rust, of dried blood, of autumn leaves nobody raked.

A year to the day, he buried it in the yard. He did not plan the date—his hands simply knew when it was time, the way hands know things bodies have not yet told the mind. He dug six inches down, near the fence line where the grass had always grown strange and patchy, and he placed the tape in the earth like a seed, like a tooth for some terrible tooth fairy, like a confession.

By the following morning, something had changed.

He does not try to explain what grew there. He has stopped trying to explain it to himself, let alone to others. What he knows is this: where he buried the tape, there rose instead a structure—beams first, then rafters, curving up like ribs, like the frame of something that wanted to be a house but became instead a gallows built by nature, a chapel with no walls. Ropes hung from the crossbeams, swaying gently though there was no wind. And in the ropes, impossibly, his father hung—not once, but many times, multiplied across the rafters like some terrible orchard bearing the same fruit again and again.

He should have been horrified. He was horrified, in the beginning. But horror, like grief, is not sustainable at its peak; it settles, the way sediment settles in water left standing. He began to visit the structure each evening, the way one might visit a grave, except a grave does not require you to look up.

A ladder extended from the highest rafter into the sky—not metaphorically, he insists, though he knows how it sounds. An actual ladder, rung after rung disappearing into cloud, into whatever waits above cloud. He never climbed it. He does not know why. Perhaps some part of him understood that ladders like this one are for descending, not ascending.

Because each night, an angel came down.

He does not describe the angel in detail—wings, perhaps, though he is vague on this point, as if the wings matter less than the tenderness. The angel descended the ladder with strips of torn tape—orange, always orange, though where this endless supply came from he never asked—and wrapped his legs with it, gently, the way one bandages a child's scraped knee. He would sit beneath the multiplying fathers and let the angel work, the tape circling his calves, his shins, adhesive catching on leg hair, and he would feel, for those minutes, held. Considered. Attended to by something that did not require him to be strong.

He never told the angel to stop. He never asked why his legs, of all places—not his chest, where the grief actually lived, not his throat, where the words got stuck. Just his legs, as if the angel understood something he did not: that a man needs his legs first, needs to be able to stand, to walk away, to carry himself out of a room before he can attend to anything happening in his chest.

But every morning, before his father's ghost-figures could stir, before the angel's tape could fully set, before anyone—including some version of himself—might wake to find the evidence, he removed it.

He unwound the tape from his legs while the light was still gray, still uncertain whether it wanted to be morning. He gathered the strips into his palm, orange going dull-copper in the half-dark, and he did not bury them. Not yet. Some other work needed doing first.

He walked to the rosemary bush that grew by the kitchen door—ordinary, green, needled and fragrant, the only plant in the yard that seemed unaware of what grew twenty feet away. He would run his hands through it, crush the small leaves between his fingers until the oil released, that sharp resinous smell like something between pine and medicine, like a kitchen and a forest arguing over which owned him.

Then he rubbed it into his hair.

This was not decoration. This was not the reflex of a man who simply enjoyed how rosemary smelled. This was ritual, though he would not have called it that—would have said, if pressed, that he was simply getting the smell of tape off his hands, the smell of nightmare off his skin. But rosemary is for remembrance, some buried part of him knew, some part that had read this once, in a poem, in a play, in his mother's garden book with the cracked spine. Rosemary, that's for remembrance. He was not trying to forget his father. He was trying to remember, instead, that he was alive—that his scalp could feel fingers, that his lungs could pull in something green and sharp and real, that the world contained plants which simply grew because the sun asked them to, without any needed history of rope or tape or coroners' bags.

Only then would he go inside. Only then would he wash his hands, make coffee, exist for the daylight hours as a man who worked a job and paid bills and answered when people asked how he was doing—fine, fine, hanging in there, and the phrase would catch in his throat every single time, a hook he'd learned to swallow past.

He never told anyone about the structure in the yard, about the fathers or the ladder or the angel with her endless tape. He knew, in the way one knows the taste of one's own blood, that this was not something explainable, not something that would survive translation into the language other people used for grief. They would suggest doctors. They would suggest medication, which perhaps he needed, which perhaps would have dissolved the whole apparatus—the beams, the ropes, the ladder climbing into whatever waited past the clouds. But he was not ready to let it dissolve. Some nights, watching the angel wrap his legs, watching his father hang in triplicate, quadruplicate, multiplied into a grove of grief, he understood that this was not punishment. This was accompaniment. This was his mind's only available way of saying: *look what he did, look what he left, look how it keeps happening, keeps happening, keeps happening*—until, each morning, the rosemary said otherwise. Until his own hands, moving through green living leaf, insisted: *but you are still here. You are still here. You are still, somehow, here.*

And so he tended two gardens at once: one that grew impossibly, nightly, in defiance of what should be possible, hung with the repeated body of his father; and one that grew ordinarily, in defiance of nothing, offering only scent, only oil, only the small mercy of being a plant that asked nothing of him except to be touched.

He has not decided which garden is more real. He has stopped trying to decide. He simply keeps removing the tape each morning, keeps walking to the rosemary, keeps rubbing green into his hair like a man anointing himself for a life he did not choose but has, somehow, agreed to keep living—one crushed leaf, one scraped strip of orange tape, one small deliberate act of return, at a time.
outputs.L5:
# A Journey Remembered

His hands trembled slightly as he opened the old wooden box, unsure of what memories it might unlock. Inside lay letters yellowed by time, photographs with curled edges, and a small brass key that fit no lock he could remember.

This was the inheritance his grandmother had left him—not wealth in the traditional sense, but fragments of a life lived fully, quietly, and with more courage than anyone had realized. Each letter told a story of resilience during difficult times, of choices made when choices were scarce, and of hope carried forward even when circumstances offered little reason for it.

From these fragments, he began to piece together a portrait of a woman he thought he knew but had never truly understood. From the careful handwriting to the pressed flowers tucked between pages, every detail revealed something new about her character, her struggles, and her unwavering determination to build a better future for those who would come after her.

As he sat there, surrounded by these remnants of the past, he realized that inheritance isn't always about what we receive—it's about what we choose to carry forward, and what we learn to value once we finally understand its worth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal narrative poem about grief after a father's suicide, using recurring images of masking tape and rope.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Tape Remembers

I.
The morning we found the note, my mother
began wrapping the house in masking tape—
strips across the doorframes, the mirror edges,
the mouth of the mailbox where his letters
still arrived like fish that didn't know
the river had been dammed.

She said it was to keep things
from falling apart at the seams.
I said the seams were already gone,
Mother. I said the house
was never sewn together
in the first place.

II.
In my dreams he is standing
in the garage, and there is rope
coiled at his feet like a sleeping animal
that loves him, that has always loved him,
patient as a dog waiting by a door.

I ask him what the rope is for
and he says *nothing, just holding things together*
and I wake up with my hands
already reaching for the tape dispenser,
already trying to bind the air.

III.
The tape does not stick to grief.
I have tested this. I have wound it
around my ribs at 3 a.m.,
around the phone that will not ring
with his voice again, around
the photographs that keep sliding
off the refrigerator like they too
are trying to leave.

Everything wants to leave.
The tape only slows the leaving down.

IV.
There is a rope in the poem now
that was not there before—
I did not put it there. It arrived
the way he arrived in the ordinary Tuesday
of my life and then did not arrive again.

The rope says: *I am not a metaphor.
I was cotton and hemp. I was purchased
at a hardware store with fluorescent lights,
paid for with actual money,
carried home in a paper bag
like something ordinary, like nails,
like a birthday candle.*

V.
My mother's hands, permanently
sticky with adhesive.
My mother, unrolling tape
across the kitchen table at midnight,
across her own knuckles,
across the photograph of the four of us
at the lake before any of this—

she is trying to keep him
from falling out of the picture.
She is trying to keep the picture
from falling out of the wall.
She is trying to keep the wall.

VI.
In the surreal logic of the after,
the rope becomes a river.
The tape becomes a bridge
made of nothing, spanning nothing,
holding up nothing but the shape
of what a bridge should do.

We cross it anyway.
We cross it every day.
Some days it holds.

VII.
This is not a poem about a rope.
This is not a poem about tape.
This is a poem about a man
who tied something and meant it,
who I loved before I knew
that love could be a room
you enter and can't leave,

and about a woman who tapes
the edges of everything now,
sealing seams that were never
going to hold, because the alternative—
the terrible, unbearable alternative—

is admitting that some things
come apart no matter
how carefully, how desperately,
how much like prayer,
you wind the tape around them.

VIII.
I keep a roll of masking tape
in my car, in my desk, in the pocket
of my winter coat. I don't know why.
Maybe I am becoming my mother.
Maybe grief just wants
a task for the hands.

Somewhere, still, in the garage
of my recurring dream, the rope
waits coiled and patient,
and I have stopped asking
what it's for.

Some questions
are just rope
pretending to be a door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in couplet-like fragments exploring a partner's inherited trauma from a parent's death, blending dreamlike and magical realism elements.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Water Remembers

You tell me your father visits in dreams still wearing his hospital slippers,
and I do not ask if this is memory or invention—only who could tell the difference.

The grief moved into your body like a tenant who never signed a lease.
It rearranges the furniture at night. You wake up bruised from walking into things that aren't there.

Your mother's hands, you said, turned to birds the week after the funeral—
not metaphor, you insisted, though I have learned not to trust the difference in your telling.

I have seen you flinch at phones ringing after midnight,
some second sense passed down like a genetic mutation, like eye color, like a curse.

In the museum of your inheritance, his death sits behind glass,
and you press your palm against the case though you know it does not warm.

Sometimes you speak in his cadences without noticing—
a stranger's inflection surfacing through your mouth like a fish coming up for air.

I have learned to recognize the days the house feels smaller,
when your grief takes up physical space, becomes a third body in our bed.

You told me once that grief skips a generation, then doubles back—
that children of the dead give birth to children who dream of hospital slippers.

I do not know if this is true. I only know I have started
setting an extra plate at dinner sometimes, without deciding to.

The dead do not stay where we put them. Yours wanders through you
into me, learning the shape of a new house to haunt.

I am building an altar in the kitchen from what you cannot say directly—
this is how I learned your father's name was Toma, how he loved the color yellow.

Some nights you wake certain someone called your name,
and I have stopped telling you that no one did. Maybe someone did.

The inheritance is this: not the grief itself but its architecture,
the rooms it built inside you before I arrived, that I am slowly learning to live in.

I hold you at 3am when the walls seem to lean closer,
when you swear you can smell his cigarettes though he's been gone eleven years.

Love, I think, is agreeing to see the birds too,
to set the extra plate, to learn the cadence, to let the dead man's grief become our weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem where an ordinary object (like masking tape) becomes a symbol of loss, growing into something surreal like trees, ladders, and angels.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Tape Dispenser

It sat on her desk like an ordinary thing,
a small tin god of silver teeth,
holding rolls of masking tape
that once sealed boxes, mended frames,
labeled jars of jam we'd never eat.

After she left, I found it
still half-fed with tape,
the last piece she'd torn
curling at the edge like a question
nobody answered.

I pulled a strip. It didn't stop.

It unspooled past my hand,
past the doorframe, past the yard,
adhesive ribbon climbing
the bark of the oak tree
until the oak became a ladder,
each rung wrapped in her fingerprints,
sticky with the ghost of her thumb.

I climbed because the tape demanded it,
because grief is architecture
built from whatever's left behind—
a spool, a smell, a habit
of reaching for what's gone.

At the top, the ladder dissolved into sky,
and there were angels made of masking tape,
translucent, humming with the sound
of boxes being sealed for the last time,
their wings not feathers but adhesive strips
peeling from some celestial roll,
sticking to nothing, holding nothing,
just the shape of holding.

One turned to me—
or maybe it was just the tape
catching light in a way that seemed like turning—
and I understood:

she is not the angel.
She is not the ladder.
She is the ordinary silver dispenser
sitting empty now,
teeth still sharp,
waiting for someone
to tear off what's left
and try, impossibly,
to hold something together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary piece about loving someone haunted by their father's suicide, incorporating garden imagery, angels, and small daily rituals of care.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Grows in Shadow

Your father left through a door that closes in you still, some mornings, when the light comes in wrong and I watch you flinch at nothing I can see. I have learned not to ask what you're seeing. I have learned instead to make the coffee, to set your cup where your hand will find it without looking.

There is a garden behind the house where nothing extraordinary grows—just tomatoes, some stubborn mint, a rose bush your mother gave us that seems to bloom out of spite more than joy. You go out there when the weight comes, and I let you go. I've stopped believing I can dig the grief out with words. Instead I kneel beside you sometimes, saying nothing, pulling weeds from soil that doesn't care what either of us has lost.

You told me once that angels are just the shape grief takes when it gets tired of being ugly. I didn't understand until I saw you standing at the kitchen window at 3 AM, moonlight making something almost holy of your exhaustion, and I thought: *there. That's what you meant.* Not wings. Not light. Just a man standing very still, carrying something too heavy for arms, made briefly beautiful by how much he was surviving.

I do not think your father was an angel when he left. I think he was just a man who ran out of rooms to hide his pain in, and mistook the last door for a mercy. You have told me this in fragments, over years, the way you'd hand someone something breakable—slowly, watching my face for signs I might drop it.

I haven't dropped it. I won't.

So: the rituals. Because love, I've learned, is mostly logistics wearing a nicer coat. It's the tea I bring you without asking, chamomile because I know the nights the news reminds you of Octobers. It's checking that the pills are counted right, not because I think you would, but because the checking is its own small prayer, a superstition against absence. It's texting *home safe?* when you're late, not from doubt but from the memory of a woman who once didn't ask that question soon enough.

The garden teaches me patience I didn't have before you. Some things take a whole season to become what they're meant to be. Your grief is like that—it doesn't bloom on my schedule, or yours. Some days you're the man who laughs at my terrible jokes, who fixes the fence, who kisses my forehead like it's an ordinary Tuesday, which it is. Other days you're standing in the yard at dusk, staring at nothing, and I bring you a sweater because the air's gone cold and this, at least, I can fix.

I do not think of myself as saving you. Saving implies a single dramatic act, a rope thrown once into water. What I do is smaller, endless: the coffee, the texts, the hand on your back when you wake gasping from dreams you won't describe. I am not your angel. I am only someone who stayed, who learned the garden's slow grammar, who understands that some grief needs tending like the tomatoes need tending—not fixed, not cured, just accompanied through each of its ordinary, necessary days.

Your father is the silence under everything we build. I have made peace with living beside that silence, the way you make peace with a house's particular creaks, the ones that used to startle you and now just mean: *this is home, and it is old, and it is still standing.*

So are you. Still standing. And when you're not, when the ground goes soft beneath you and you feel yourself sinking toward whatever door he found—I am here, digging beside you in a garden that keeps growing anyway, keeps insisting on green, keeps offering us small stubborn proof:

that some things left in the dark still find their way toward light.

That tending is a kind of faith.

That I am not leaving.

That this, at least, this small daily grace of tea and texts and hands finding hands in the dark—

this, at least, I can give you, over and over, for as long as it takes the wound to soften into scar, the scar into simply *skin*, the skin into simply *you*, whole and here and mine to love, exactly as you are, exactly as he could not stay to be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an experimental poem using slashes for line breaks, focusing on themes of memory, mourning, and the body's connection to the dead.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Body Keeps**

i touch my collarbone and find / your fingerprint still pressed there / like a coin flattened on a track / long after the train has gone /

the doctor says grief lives in the chest / but mine has moved into the hands / they open drawers looking for you / they fold laundry the way you did / crease by crease / small mourning rituals / no one taught me to perform /

your voice is a bone that healed wrong / now every word i speak / bends slightly toward you / i have started talking to the ceiling / because it is closer to where you might be /

//

they say the body forgets pain / but mine remembers yours / the weight of you against my shoulder / a phantom limb / except the limb was never mine to lose /

i keep finding your name / in my mouth like a stone i sucked as a child / to stop the hunger / it does not stop the hunger /

we are made of the same water / this is not metaphor / this is chemistry / this is why my eyes still leak / your salt / your tide / your going out and out and out /

//

at the funeral they dressed you / in a color you never wore / i wanted to say / that isn't him / that isn't the shirt that smelled like cut grass and cigarettes / but grief makes liars of the living / we agree to bury / a stranger in your clothes /

//

six months later i find your hair / still in the drain / i do not clean it / i let the water pool around it / like a small grieving / like a river that refuses / to remember its own mouth /

//

somewhere my hands are still reaching / for a door that isn't there / somewhere my body keeps setting / two plates at the table /

i am learning the grammar of your absence / how you are always / present tense / in the wrong place / how memory conjugates / into ache / into ache / into ache /

//

if the body is an archive / then i am overdue / for every book you left unread / every name you called me / softly / like a hand closing / over a flame /

i keep the flame / i keep it / lit / in the small room / behind my ribs / where you used to / live /
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
